data.name: Bahrain
data.summary: No personal income tax, no capital gains tax, no tax on dividends or interest, no wealth tax and no inheritance or estate tax. No general corporate tax (46% on oil and gas; 15% DMTT for MNE groups with EUR 750m+ revenue from 2025). VAT 10%. Real estate transfers carry 2% stamp duty (1.7% if paid within two months). About 50 treaties, none with the US.

wealth_tax.property_tax_note: No general property tax. A 10% municipality tax applies to rent on property let to expatriates (paid by the owner); this is a rental levy, not a wealth tax.

inheritance.summary: No inheritance, estate or gift tax.
inheritance.important_exceptions: Succession, not tax, is the issue: personal status (family) law based on Sharia governs inheritance of Muslims, with fixed shares (a son typically takes twice a daughter's share) and at most one third freely disposable by will to non-heirs. How estates of non-Muslim foreigners are handled (home-country law, own religious rules, or Sharia by default) was not verified for this country; non-Muslim families should take local legal advice and hold portfolio assets outside the country or through a structure with a clear governing law.

income.name: Bahrain

income_tax.summary: Bahrain has no personal income tax (PwC, reviewed 26 Jul 2026). Employees in Bahrain contribute to the Social Insurance Organisation: expatriates pay 1% (employer 3%), Bahrainis 8% (employer 18%). Income paid outside Bahrain is not subject to Bahraini tax or social insurance rules.
income_tax.self_employed_notes: Self-employed contributions are not covered by the PwC page; none are assumed. Foreign-paid income is outside the Bahraini social insurance rules.

succession.name: Bahrain
succession.summary: Muslims are governed by Sharia, which guarantees fixed shares; the Constitution (art. 5(d)) makes inheritance a right governed by Islamic Sharia. Non-Muslim foreigners are governed by the law of their own country under Legislative Decree 11 of 1971. Bahrain has a trust law, but the sources found do not settle foundations.
succession.reserved_share: Muslims: fixed Sharia shares (Constitution art. 5(d); Bahrain's family law is largely uncodified and applied case by case by the Sharia courts). Bequests are limited to one third under Sharia (not sourced for Bahrain).
succession.foreign_law_note: Legislative Decree 11 of 1971 on the inheritance and settlement of estates of non-Muslim aliens applies the law of the deceased's country to identify heirs and their shares; with no heirs, the estate goes to the Bahraini Treasury after a year. It applies to non-Muslim foreigners by operation of law, not as a free choice. A Muslim foreigner's estate would follow Sharia.
succession.trust_note: Bahrain has a statutory trust law (reported as Legislative Decree 23 of 2006; number not verified) used for family business planning. Whether Sharia shares can be overridden by a trust over a Muslim's Bahraini assets is untested in the sources found. No private-foundation statute was found (waqf exists for Muslims).
open_questions: Verify the Bahrain trust law's number and scope; the Tamimi article could not be retrieved in full.
No source found on a private foundation law; 'no' is provisional.
Bahraini Supreme Court 2026 decision on foreign Jewish customs in succession (conflictoflaws.net) not read in full.

Hague Trusts Convention: The HCCH status table (checked 2026-10-16) lists 14 Contracting Parties; this country is not one of them and no UK, Dutch or Chinese extension covers it, so the 1985 Convention is not in force here.

immigration.name: Bahrain
immigration.summary: No free movement for anyone; EU, US and other passports use the same Golden Residency categories (Resolution 20 of 2022): property (BHD 130,000 since the NPRA announcement of 26 November 2025, still BHD 200,000 on the portal page), employees with 5 years' residence and BHD 2,000 salary, retirees, and talented individuals. No remote-work visa was found. Citizenship is not realistically open.
immigration.naturalisation: Not researched from the Bahraini Nationality Law in this pass. Golden Residency does not lead to citizenship.
immigration.dual_citizenship_note: General rule, not verified in this pass: Bahrain does not generally allow dual nationality for naturalised citizens.

routes.name: Golden Residency - property owners
routes.summary: Own Bahraini property worth at least BHD 130,000 and get a 10-year renewable residence without a sponsor.
routes.requirements: NPRA announced on 26 November 2025 a cut of the minimum from BHD 200,000 to BHD 130,000. The Bahrain National Portal page (undated) still says title deed value of at least BHD 200,000. Documents: valid health insurance in Bahrain, passport valid 6+ months, title deed, 6-month bank statement. Processing 5 working days.
routes.fees_note: BHD 5 application (non-refundable) plus BHD 300 for the 10-year permit.
routes.physical_presence: Not stated on the portal; one source reports 90 days a year (unconfirmed).
routes.family: Spouse, children and parents can be included (secondary source).
routes.tax_note: Bahrain has no personal income tax.

routes.name: Golden Residency - employees living in Bahrain
routes.summary: Residents with 5 years in Bahrain and a salary of at least BHD 2,000 a month can switch to a 10-year Golden Residency.
routes.requirements: NPRA: 5 years of residence in Bahrain and average basic salary of at least BHD 2,000 over the last 5 years (portal wording; salary certificate shows minimum BHD 2,000). Documents: health insurance, 6-month bank statement. Processing 5 working days.
routes.fees_note: BHD 5 plus BHD 300 every 10 years. Income is BHD 2,000 a month x 12; the period is monthly per secondary sources, not stated on the NPRA page.
routes.tax_note: Bahrain has no personal income tax.
